title: Review on the impact of processing routes and external factors on phase formation and tribological properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs
abstract: Abstract High-entropy alloys (HEAs) based on CoCrFeMnNi continue to attract attention to their balanced mechanical properties and corrosion resistance; however, their tribological response remains strongly path-dependent. This review combines processing routes such as casting, powder metallurgy/spark plasma sintering (SPS), additive manufacturing (SLM/LPBF), and coating methods such as PVD/thermal spray with the resultant phase constitution (FCC, BCC, σ, and Laves) and defect structures to describe their trends in hardness, friction, and wear at room temperature up to approximately 800 o C. To balance different literature reports, we standardize the units of wear and cluster complete test data (counterface, load, kinematics, atmosphere, and temperature) so that quantitative comparison between studies is possible. Determining (i) systematic decreases when the FCC changes to BCC or intermetallic-reinforced state and (ii) a crossover in temperature at which many coating types can minimize wear at approximately 400 o C before increasing in temperature, a causal map was constructed linking route-controlled phase selection and secondary reinforcers (e.g., carbides/solid lubricants) to effect sizes in selective wear and friction. A route-selection guide, important information gaps in tribocorrosion (sliding-electrochemistry coupling), and template reporting tools that improve design and reproducibility are included at the conclusion of the review. All these factors lead to a consistent foundation on which to build the engineering of Cantor based HEAs and coating to meet desired wear windows in commercial environments.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Material is very important in human civilization development due to the technological level and the continuous need for better material. In 1995, the concept of designing alloys under the name of High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) transformed the design of alloys by providing a new idea that was quite broad in comparison with the previous techniques [ 1 ]. Multi-principal alloys, also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), are multi-principal elements and are a recent addition to the family of structural application materials [ 2 ,  3 ]. The concept of the new alloy design paradigm was initially suggested by Cantor et al. [ 4 ] and Yeh et al. [ 1 ] in 2004, and since that time HEAs have become the focus of the area of attention of the metals structural material. The HEAs overcome the historical idea of alloy design varying based on one or two key elements and purposefully adds small quantities of alloying elements to improve properties [ 1 ,  4 ] thereby, an extended array of uses can be expanded [ 5 ].

The proposed compositions by Yeh et al. [ 6 ] can be described as HEAs, where the composition is composed of at least 5 major metallic elements with near-equimolar ratios, each of which is between 5 and 35 (atomic percentage) [ 7 ,  8 ]. Unlike traditional concepts of physical metallurgy, HEAs utilize high mixing entropy effect to essentially form one solid-solution structure, as opposed to the anticipated intermetallic compounds [ 9 ]. Moreover, properly designed HEAs are capable of spontaneously producing nano-scale precipitates or even amorphous structures without the need to use any advanced processing method [ 10 ,  11 ]. The forming and processing procedures of HEAs are important factors that determine their microstructure and general features, and it is possible to make important changes by a careful choice of elements and thermomechanical processing methods [ 5 ]. Such alloys are characterized by outstanding mechanical characteristics, particularly strength and hardness [ 1 ,  12 ,  13 ], great wear resistance [ 14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 ,  20 ,  21 – 22 ] and resistance to softening under high temperatures [ 23 ]. HEAs have multiple applications in practice because of their remarkable properties. They can also be used in hydrogen storage [ 23 ], as efficient diffusion barriers [ 23 ], and even researched as biomedical applications due to their corrosion resistance and biocompatibility [ 24 ,  25 ,  26 ,  27 – 28 ]. Along with the increased attention focused on creation and characterization of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), tribological research on friction and wear behaviour of these materials has also gained momentum [ 29 ]. According to Vaidya et al. [ 29 ], tribology publications have grown in the last five to six years in tandem with the increase of studies overall related to HEA. Tribology, which involves the science of friction, wear, and lubrication, is important in determining the service behavior of structural materials. Newly designed HEAs, with their outstanding hardness, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, have further increased the list of wear-resistant alloys [ 29 ]. Although there has been an increasing interest in this area, there have been limited literature reviews that have summarized tribological results. Because material wear is one of the key causes of mechanical failure, more studies are required to have a better understanding of these alloys and inform the selection of materials to use in industries. The aim of this review is to summarise and synthesise the available tribological research of HEAs and provide an insight that can guide metallurgists in enhancing tribology-specific alloy development research. The focus of this work is the effect of various processing strategies and other external factors on phase formation and tribological characteristics in CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Research activities with respect to tribology of these alloys under different environmental conditions have been taken into consideration. The reviewed materials can be classified according to their crystal structures: face-centered cubic (FCC) and FCC + body-centered cubic (BCC) because these phases are the most common ones in ingot-cast CoCrFeMnNi HEAs [ 29 ,  30 ]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) based on CoCrFeMnNi are a well-researched family whose single-phase FCC state provides corrosion resistance and toughness. However, engineering these materials for wear-intensive and friction-intensive applications necessitates careful control over phase constitution and microstructure, which are extremely sensitive to alloying strategy and processing route. Practical selection and processing decisions require a synthesis that emphasize tribology rather than just strength or ductility. However, to design such materials to have friction and wear intensive applications, it is necessary to control phase constitution and microstructure, which are very sensitive to processing route and alloying strategy. An overview of tribology that anticipates instead of just strength or ductility should be made to inform sensible selection and processing choices.

However, the impact of processing methods on HEA properties remains debated, and no clear consensus has been reached regarding their tribological performance in extreme conditions. While multiple studies have attempted to address this uncertainty, high-temperature tribology remains an underexplored area. This review assembles results across casting, PM/SPS, additive manufacturing (SLM/LPBF), and coating technologies (PVD/thermal spray) to explain route-dependent thermal histories, defect content, and chemical partitioning steer phase evolution among FCC, BCC, σ, and laves. By normalizing wear metrics and compiling complete test metadata for pin-/ball-on-disc and reciprocating configurations, we expose consistent patterns in friction and wear and connect them to hardness and oxide-film development at temperature.

In tribology-first lens: (i) single-phase FCC Cantor variants frequently occupy the upper band of specific wear at room temperature, (ii) BCC conversion and intermetallic reinforcement reduce wear by multiples under comparable kinematics, and (iii) several coatings show a distinct minimum near ~ 400 °C followed by deterioration as oxide scales coarsen or spall. These observations motivate route-selection guidance and identify the need for coupled tribocorrosion measurements that reflect service environments.

The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy, known as the Cantor alloy, has occurred as one of the most extensively explored compositions. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), particularly the FCC-dominated CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy), have emerged as promising materials due to their excellent thermal stability, corrosion resistance, and mechanical properties [ 31 ,  32 ,  33 ,  34 – 35 ]. This alloy exhibits tensile strength above 1 GPa and elongation exceeding 70%, accommodating severe deformation through abundant slip systems and deformation twinning, which enhance dislocation activity, plastic deformation, and ductility [ 36 ,  37 ]. However, its tribological performance deteriorates above ~ 800 °C due to adhesive wear and unstable oxide scales, while grain boundary decohesion at elevated temperatures can cause intergranular fracture, reducing tensile strength and ductility [ 38 ,  39 – 40 ]. Therefore, incorporating high-temperature solid lubricants into the alloy matrix is essential to improve tribological performance under extreme conditions.

The CoCrFeMnNi Cantor alloy, a typical face-centered cubic (FCC) HEA, is widely recognized for its exceptional fracture toughness, ductility at cryogenic temperatures, good plasticity, machinability, and corrosion resistance [ 41 ,  42 ,  43 ,  44 – 45 ]. The stability and performance of HEAs originate from key effects such as high configurational entropy, sluggish diffusion, and severe lattice distortion, which enhance mechanical strength and thermal stability [ 46 ]. Consequently, HEAs with FCC, body-centered cubic (BCC), and dual-phase structures have been extensively explored for advanced applications in aerospace, biomedical implants, and energy systems [ 43 ,  47 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ].

The improved wear resistance of CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs, makes them promising candidates for engineering applications involving severe tribological conditions, including various aerospace moving components, tooling systems, marine hardware, and energy-sector equipment [ 51 ]. In particular, the ability to tailor wear resistance through processing (e.g., grain refinement, phase transformation) and compositional design (e.g., oxide-forming elements) enables their deployment in high strength, elevated temperature, and hars corrosive environments, where conventional alloys often fail. Recent studies on HEA composites and coatings further demonstrate their potential for surface engineering applications, such as protective coatings and additive-manufactured wear-resistant layers [ 43 ,  47 ,  48 ,  49 – 50 ].

Although several reviews have discussed the general properties of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), including the widely studied CoCrFeMnNi system, most of the existing literature primarily focuses on fundamental alloy design principles, phase stability, or mechanical properties, while comparatively fewer studies systematically examine the tribological performance in relation to processing routes and microstructural evolution. Furthermore, the rapid growth of research on CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs in recent years—particularly with the emergence of advanced processing techniques such as additive manufacturing, laser surface engineering, spark plasma sintering, and thermal spraying—has generated a substantial amount of new experimental data that is not comprehensively covered in earlier reviews [ 52 ]. In addition, many previous reviews discuss wear behavior only briefly or treat tribological performance as a secondary property without establishing a clear processing–microstructure–tribological property relationship.

The evolution of research on CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys over the past two decades is summarized in Fig.  1 , highlighting the rapid expansion of studies related to processing technologies and tribological applications in recent years. Early research focused on fundamental alloy design and mechanical properties, while recent studies increasingly address tribological performance, advanced processing routes, and high-temperature applications. sections.heading: Comparative tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs and nickel-based superalloys
paragraphs: In comparison, the CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (often referred to as the Cantor alloy) is characterized by a stable single-phase FCC solid-solution structure and high configurational entropy, which contributes to excellent mechanical stability and deformation mechanisms such as dislocation slip and twinning under tribological loading [ 54 ]. During sliding wear, CoCrFeMnNi HEAs typically exhibit adhesive wear, oxidative wear, and delamination mechanisms depending on contact conditions and counterface materials [ 55 ,  56 ].

Overall, while nickel-based superalloys offer superior high-temperature reliability, the CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy provides a promising alternative due to its compositional flexibility, good wear resistance, and microstructural stability [ 57 ]. Therefore, HEAs are increasingly investigated for advanced tribological systems and may complement or partially replace conventional superalloys in future engineering applications.

The tribological data summarized in Table  1  are compiled from representative studies on CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys and nickel-based superalloys reported in the literature. These studies indicate that HEAs typically exhibit friction coefficients in the range of 0.25–0.6, with wear mechanisms dominated by adhesive and oxidative wear, whereas nickel-based superalloys generally show friction coefficients of 0.3–0.5 with stable wear behavior at elevated temperatures due to oxide film formation and precipitation strengthening. This study presents the first comprehensive review focused on the tribological behavior of Cantor alloy systems, systematically correlating processing routes, phase formation, and tribological performance. In this review, a distinction is made between: (i) processing-route-dependent effects, which govern microstructural attributes such as grain size, phase fraction, defect density, and residual stress; and (ii) composition-dependent effects, including elemental partitioning and alloying modifications that influence intrinsic phase stability and deformation mechanisms. The novelty of this work lies in integrating major fabrication techniques within a unified framework and emphasizing reproducibility through coordinated units, complete metadata, and a compact reporting template applicable to both bulk and coated CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs, providing a structured reference for future tribological research. Consequently, this work serves not only as an updated overview of the rapidly expanding literature, but also as a useful reference for researchers and engineers seeking to develop high-performance HEA materials for industrial wear applications.

sections.heading: Various fabrication techniques of high entropy alloys
paragraphs: In this review different fabrication techniques of high entropy alloys are discussed in Fig.  2 . The manufacturing methods are generally classified into two primary categories: melting techniques and powder metallurgy processes [ 7 ,  60 ,  61 ]. Vacuum arc melting (VAM) and vacuum induction melting (VIM) are recognized as the predominant techniques for processing HEAs [ 60 ]. Conversely, mechanical alloying (MA) followed by sintering represents the primary solid-state processing method employed to produce sintered HEA products. Fig. 2 Flow Chart of fabrication techniques

Each fabrication technique influencing the material’s properties [ 62 ]. The choice of fabrication techniques is essential for optimizing the final product’s properties to meet specific application requirements [ 63 ] such as aerospace and automotive to advanced materials engineering [ 64 ].

High-Entropy Alloys are available in various forms, including ingots, slabs, powders, and thin films. There are typically two main manufacturing techniques which are melting techniques and powder metallurgy techniques [ 7 ,  60 ,  61 ]. They are considered to be vacuum arc melting (VAM) and vacuum induction melting (VIM) as the most common methods of processing HEAs [ 60 ].

sections.heading: Arc melting process
paragraphs: Arc melting is a typical process used to produce HEAs, but it may be cost-effectively inefficient and constrained in the ability to shape finished products [ 65 ,  66 ]. In order to resolve such problems as porosity and uneven mixing during the casting, sintering the alloy powders prior to remelting may be used [ 67 ]. This is done by melting powders or ingots of alloy in a crucible with the help of the tungsten arc that is ignited in an atmosphere of inert gas in a vacuum to avoid oxidation [ 60 ].

Figure  3 , which is a representation of a typical arc melting area demonstrates that AM technique can be applied in the melting of alloy powders or ingots using a metallic crucible. Electrode temperature in an arc melting furnace may reach up to 3000 °C and thus liquefy a majority of the elements used to make HEAs. The level of temperature can be adjusted too with the help of electrical power. Arc melting is especially useful in refracting high-melting-point elements, such as refractory elements, because of these high temperatures, which provide even melt mixing [ 60 ]. Cantor et al. [ 68 ] also showed that melt spinning alloys based on equiatomic quinary and six elements, including CoCrFeMnNi, CoCrFeMnNiNb, CoCrFeMnNiTi, CoCrFeMnNiV, CoCrFeMnNiCu and CoCrFeMnNiGe usually results in a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) structure. This implies that higher cooling rates prevent the formation of secondary phases and have single-phase alloys [ 4 ]. Fig. 3 Arc melting process [ 69 ]

Microwave heating and sintering can also enhance the microstructure and mechanical properties of HEAs to that of conventional heating methods and require less power [ 67 ]. In comparison to melting and casting methods, processes that increase the rate of solidification, including splat quenching, melt spinning, injection casting, suction casting, and drop casting, have similar microstructures composed chiefly of single-phase structures. Moreover, they make use of vacuum arc melting to produce refractory high-entropy alloys, which affect their structural and mechanical characteristics based on the alloy composition [ 70 ]. Hardness and yield strength can be increased by adjusting the Cr level in the HEAs formed by vacuum arc welding and suction casting [ 71 ].

sections.heading: Melt spinning technique
paragraphs: Melt spinning is a fast solidification method in which molten metals are cooled at very high rates to retain the structure of the liquid and produce an amorphous or highly disordered solid. This method gives metallic glass, in which the temperatures of glass transition and crystallization can be distinguished. Melt spinning can be used to ensure that unwanted phases do not develop in case of the formation of crystalline materials [ 72 ]. The level of undercooling is regulated by varying the speed of rotation of the wheel, resulting in a finer grain structure, commonly of the micrometer scale [ 72 ]. In the case of High Entropy Alloys (HEAs), melt spinning is used in which a jet of molten metal is thrown onto a rapidly rotating copper wheel, which quickly solidifies into thin ribbons. Because of such high cooling rates, the obtained material may have nanocrystalline or amorphous structure, which makes this method very efficient in refining HEA microstructures and reducing phase segregation [ 72 ].

sections.heading: Solid-state processing techniques
paragraphs: HEAs with improved mechanical, physical, and chemical properties are produced using solid-state processing methods, such as mechanical alloying [ 73 ,  74 ]. These methods continually give nanocrystalline grains and alloying elements with extensive melting point disparities, influencing the phases, microstructure, oxidation items, and mass gain kinetics of the HEA [ 73 ]. Surface treatments such as electrolytic polishing, electro erosive machining and mechanical polishing are also used to alter the surface characteristics of HEAs [ 73 ].

sections.heading: Powder metallurgy
paragraphs: Powder metallurgy (PM) provides a highly adaptable and inexpensive pathway to HEA development, and through the control of composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties [ 75 ,  76 ]. The method yields special HEAs, and gives special compositions, the properties of which are quite competitive with those of ingot casting [ 77 ]. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) is a prominent PM methodology of HEAs, since it permits quick heating at lesser temperatures and less sintering duration [ 61 ,  75 ,  78 ,  79 ,  80 ,  81 ,  82 ,  83 – 84 ]. PM can be subjected to microwave-assisted methods to achieve short alloying periods and efficient cooling, but this method can lead to increased residual porosity [ 60 ,  85 ]. Mechanical alloying (MA) is also a common route for HEA fabrication, enhancing the solubility of elements [ 73 ,  86 ,  87 ,  88 ,  89 – 90 ]. It is a high-energy ball milling technique” for blending elemental powders to form a homogeneous alloy through atomic diffusion [ 90 ]. Originally developed by Benjamin et al. in 1970 “to produce oxide dispersion-strengthened Ni-base superalloys” [ 91 ]. MA gained further prominence in 1990 when Fecht et al. used it to synthesize nanocrystalline metals [ 92 ]. High-energy milling deforms, fractures, and welds particles, ultimately enabling nano crystallization or even amorphization. Over the past four decades, MA has become a reliable method for producing diverse advanced materials, including nanomaterials, Intermetallic, quasicrystals, amorphous materials, and nanocomposites [ 93 ,  94 – 95 ]. Additive manufacturing techniques, such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), are widely used for net-shape fabrication of HEAs [ 96 ]. It enables the production of complex HEA components and allows for tailoring of alloy microstructures [ 97 ,  98 – 99 ]. Nevertheless, microstructural flaws in HEAs manufactured through L-PBF usually require further heat treatment to be optimized [ 96 ]. Additional techniques of Additive Manufacturing are selective laser melting (SLM) [ 100 ,  101 ,  102 ,  103 – 104 ], electron beam melting (EBM) [ 105 ], directed energy deposition (DED) [ 106 ,  107 ] and additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) [ 108 ].

sections.heading: Selective laser melting (SLM)
paragraphs: Selective Laser Melting is a superior additive manufacturing technique that allows the creation of complex High Entropy Alloy (HEA) parts through the selective deviation of layers of metal powder with a high-powered laser [ 102 ,  103 – 104 ]. The methodology allows obtaining geometrically complicated structures with better mechanical properties because of the unique multi-element structure of HEAs [ 102 ,  103 ]. SLM is especially beneficial in producing HEA components with desirable microstructures and high performing which, in many cases, are difficult to produce using traditional manufacturing methods [ 103 ,  109 ,  110 – 111 ].

sections.heading: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)
paragraphs: Another potential additive manufacturing technique is Laser Powder Bed Fusion which has enormous potential to produce HEAs with customized microstructural properties and with high level of mechanical performance [ 96 ,  112 ,  113 ]. The fast cooling and ability to accurately control the parameters involved in the laser-based process favor formation of fine-grained uniform structures that cannot be easily formed using traditional fabrication methods. After all, it facilitates the designing of HEA components of higher strength, toughness, and wear resistance, which is why it is a useful method to apply high-performance materials [ 96 ,  112 ,  113 ].

sections.heading: Physical vapor deposition techniques (PVD)
paragraphs: The use of physical vapor deposition to produce HEA thin film and coatings makes the atomic radius mismatch a key design and synthesis parameter [ 114 ]. Coating interventions on surface materials such as stainless steels and titanium alloys are applied by various PVD techniques such as magnetron sputtering, thermal sputtering and laser sputtering [ 115 ]. Another Vapor deposition method is metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) which is applied in the manufacture of high speed electronic and optoelectronic gadgets. A new method to fabricate lightweight HEAs in air at atmospheric pressure is investigated through the pulsed laser deposition (PLD), and the impact of the laser wavelength is considered [ 116 ].

sections.heading: Influence of processing techniques on the phase formation, microstructure, mechanical and tribological properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs
paragraphs: The processing methods play a significant role in shaping the phase formation, microstructure, mechanical properties and tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [ 84 ,  117 ,  118 ,  119 ,  120 ,  121 – 122 ]. With their complex compositions, these alloys are disposable to multiple applications as they have a wide variety of material properties [ 51 ].

sections.heading: Effect of processing routes on the CoCrFeMnNi HEA
paragraphs: Some of the methods used to make CoCrFeMnNi HEAs include conventional casting, melt-spinning, mechanical alloying, and modern ones that include SLM and LPBF. Both processes have their unique benefits and obstacles which determine the microstructure and mechanical characteristics [ 121 ]. SLM is particularly known to exhibit high strength and ductility in those alloys based on C, which makes it suitable to be used in high-performance applications [ 121 ,  123 ]. Powder metallurgy and induction melting are the new methods that are used to manufacture high-entropy alloys.

In the future, processes that involve better techniques than ball-milling will be employed to manufacture HEA powders and the environment of SPS will be optimized to reduce the growth of grains and enhance the solidity of the grain boundaries [ 61 ,  64 ,  79 ]. Milling and sintering CoCrFeMnNi HEA results in significant increase in hardness in contrast to the conventional melting and casting techniques [ 124 ].

The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy (Cantor alloy) has gained significant attention due to its excellent mechanical performance over a wide temperature range and its ability to maintain structural integrity under extreme conditions [ 141 ,  142 – 143 ]. These properties make it a promising material for applications in aerospace, nuclear reactors, and cryogenic environments [ 144 ,  145 – 146 ]. However, conventional processing techniques often face challenges such as poor machinability, elemental segregation, and limited geometric flexibility when fabricating HEAs [ 140 ,  147 ,  148 ,  149 – 150 ].

Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) has emerged as an effective alternative, enabling near-net-shape fabrication, high design freedom, and rapid solidification, which promotes grain refinement and improved chemical homogeneity [ 151 ,  152 ]. Nevertheless, process-induced defects such as porosity, voids, and residual thermal stresses may still occur, affecting mechanical reliability [ 153 ]. Despite these challenges, L-PBF demonstrates strong potential as a scalable and defect-controllable manufacturing route for high-performance CoCrFeMnNi HEA components, offering improved structural homogeneity and mechanical reliability for advanced applications in aerospace, biomedical implants, and extreme service environments [ 154 ,  155 – 156 ].

sections.heading: Influence on phase formation
paragraphs: The phase formation in CoCrFeMnNi HEAs is affected by processing techniques such as spark plasma sintering, thermal treatment, and the addition of certain elements [ 118 ,  119 ,  163 ,  164 ].For instance, adding silicon can promote the formation of the σ phase. Also, the amount of chromium influences phase formation [ 119 ].High-temperature processing and controlled cooling rates are required for the entropy-driven formation of HEA materials [ 133 ]. Table  2 . Shows the phase evolved after different processing route in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA. Processing routes significantly affect the phase evolution and mechanical properties of CoCrCuFeNiSix HEAs; the addition of Si encourages the formation of the σ phase [ 118 ]. Melting routes for processing CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi HEAs result in a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure [ 163 ]. Severe plastic deformation can result in the formation of a NiMn phase and a Cr-rich phase with increased annealing temperature [ 161 ]. Different powder metallurgy routes have successfully produced CoCrFeMnNi HEAs [ 165 ].Various processing routes, including vacuum arc melting, have been employed to prepare HEAs [ 166 ]. Processing maps can be developed to understand the hot workability of HEAs [ 167 ]. HEAs can be manufactured using processing routes like conventional liquid phase sintering, microwave sintering, and spark plasma sintering [ 168 ]. Machine learning techniques, specifically artificial neural networks, are being used to predict phase formation by using datasets with balanced data for each phase [ 51 ,  169 ].

sections.heading: Influence on microstructure
paragraphs: Thermo-mechanical processing, heating rates and severe plastic deformation can affect the microstructure development of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs [ 168 ,  170 ,  171 – 172 ]. Initial grains size affects microstructure and texture in thermo-mechanical processing [ 172 ]. Heavy deformation can be done to get ultrafine microstructures [ 172 ]. Microstructure and texture also depend on the rate of heating during annealing [ 172 ]. Moreover, alloys design could be obtained by means of single-phase solid solutions [ 172 ]. To ensure that brittle precipitates are reduced to a minimum, especially σ-phase, it is important to control the processing pathway to ensure the mechanical properties of HEAs are not diminished. In order to reduce the formation of brittle precipitates especially the sigma -phase, it is important to control the processing pathway to preserve the mechanical properties of HEAs [ 172 ].

sections.heading: Influence on mechanical properties
paragraphs: The heat treatments, processing parameters and element addition influence the mechanical properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs [ 118 ,  173 ,  174 – 175 ]. These alloys may be prepared by metal injection molding (MIM) and hot isostatic pressing (HIP), HIP enhancing the properties of MIM samples by removing pores [ 176 ]. There are also effects of laser surface heat treatment on the mechanical properties [ 176 ]. Table  2 . Displays the mechanical qualities through various processing paths in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA. Inclusion of titanium influences the microstructure and mechanical properties, and the environment is a mixture of FCC solid solution dendrites and intermetallic phases [ 176 ]. Selective laser melting could improve the mechanical properties through the generation of many strengthening mechanisms [ 176 ,  177 ].

CoCrFeMnNi HEAs have different mechanical properties when different processing techniques are used. The samples processed by SLM usually have better yield strength and elongation of samples because of the microstructure that is produced due to a high rate of cooling and a high input of energy [ 176 ]. As an example, HEAs manufactured by SLM exhibit improved tensile strength than cast samples, which is explained by higher dislocation density and nanoscale precipitates that refine the microstructure [ 96 ]. The approach reduced the coarse-grained cast structure to a fine-grained cast (approximately 50 nm), which occurred with a strength of 1950 MPa and a hardness of 520 HV [ 176 ]. CoCrFeMnNi HEA equiatomic made by SLM shows excellent mechanical properties at room temperature to high temperatures. Some factors leading to this phenomenon include size of fine grains and dislocation networks, and nano-sized oxides. Dislocation forest hardening and Orowan strengthening are the primary processes that occur at high temperatures. Moreover, deformation at 600 °C showed type-C serration, which was likely due to the interaction between constituent elements and dislocations [ 176 ].

sections.heading: Thermal properties
paragraphs: Processing routes affect the thermal properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. The thermodynamic process of rapid cooling of 3D printing methods such as SLM forms a non-equilibrium microstructure, which improves thermal stability and behavior in high-temperature conditions. On the contrary, the terms of thermal properties can vary with materials produced by conventional techniques, and the fabrication process should be well chosen to meet the requirements of high thermal load [ 112 ].

sections.heading: Comparative strength analysis
paragraphs: Comparative experiments reveal that CoCrFeMnNi HEAs performances are very sensitive to the processing way. Alloyed samples obtained by mechanical alloying and by spark plasma sintering (SPS) have much greater hardness and strength than alloyed samples obtained by casting. Also, SLM and LPBF offer accurate microstructure control, which can be used to customize properties to meet certain application requirements [ 104 ].

sections.heading: Impact on corrosion resistance
paragraphs: CoCrFeMnNi HEAs are influenced by the processing method on their corrosion resistance. Research indicates that additively manufactured HEAs such as SLM exhibit superior corrosion resistance because of better elemental distribution and reduced porosity than traditional cast alloys, which is why they can be used in corrosive environments [ 25 ,  128 ,  178 ].​CoCrFeMnNi HEAs are also greatly influenced by their fabrication paths that greatly affect their micro structures and mechanical characteristics which determine their applicability in high performance applications [ 128 ,  179 ].

All wear rates reported are normalized to mm³N⁻¹ m⁻¹ and reported with test metadata (counter face, diameter, load and speed/frequency, distance/time, temperature and atmosphere) to facilitate cross-study comparison. This harmonized dataset and a route→phase→hardness→ wear→mechanism infographic allows readers to observe the quantitative impact of alloying, processing route and reinforcement type.

Enhancement of solid solutions mainly takes place between the solute and interstitial atoms [ 198 ,  199 – 200 ]. Also, strength of the alloy can be improved by the occurrence of secondary phase, or intermetallic compounds. As an example, adding vanadium to CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) results in the appearance of σ and other FCC phases, which give rise to hardness and yield strength [ 201 ]. In the same manner, a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure is obtained by the addition of aluminum [ 202 ]. The use of a second phase of reinforcing HEAs by means of incorporating ceramic particles is a good approach to enhance strength. The Cr 3 C 2  phase which is characterized by very high hardness, thermal stability, and high temperature strength is also better wear resistant and improved mechanical properties but has been less researched. Concerning the fabrication techniques, CoCrFeNiMn HEAs are usually prepared via vacuum arc melting [ 142 ]. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) is a useful method to overcome the problem of alloy segregation as it involves the activation of plasma, the field of electric force, and hot pressing, which allow the high-speed and homogeneous densification without delays [ 182 ,  203 ].

Incorporating Cr₃C₂ into CoCrFeNiMn HEA during sintering resulted in the formation of FCC and Cr₇C₃ phases, which improved its tribological performance [ 182 ]. In the absence of Cr 3 C 2 , the alloy had a Vickers hardness of 181.2 HV. Nonetheless, the hardness with 10, 20, and 40% Cr 3 C 2  were 323.2, 417.0, and 681.6 HV respectively. Friction coefficient decreased with temperature as a result of the joint action of oxide layer lubrication and softening of the matrix and reached a minimum at 20% Cr 3 C 2  and after that, it started to increase again at 40%.

Figure  6 a indicates that the coefficient of friction of CoCrFeNiMn HEA was 0.62 at a room temperature that continued to decrease with increase in temperatures to 200, 400, 600 and 800 °C. Also, as indicated by Fig.  6 b, the addition of Cr 3 C 2  significantly reduced the wear rate, where the maximum wear resistance was noted at 10% Cr 3 C 2  throughout the entire temperature ranges between 800 °C and 25 °C [ 182 ]. Recent research has also examined the performance of face-centered cubic (FCC) HEAs wear [ 159 ,  188 ,  204 ], such as a popular Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) [ 4 ,  205 ]. Although these alloys exhibit very good tensile ductility and fracture toughness owing to the twinning mechanisms, the low yield strength is a constraint in use in some applications [ 142 ,  206 ]. Wear studies conducted by Nagarjuna et al. [ 188 ] carried out wear studies on Cantor alloy through ball-on-disc dry sliding test. To start with, there were small scratches and adhering debris on the surface of alloy (Fig.  7 (a)). In the case where the stress on the contact was high, surface cracking was formed, and delamination was induced further (Fig.  7 (b) and (c)). With an increase in contact stress, surface cracks were formed and later delamination occurred. These results show that there is a gradual change between abrasive and adhesive wear to delamination with time. Dollmann et al. [ 188 ], found hardening of the strains, and surface hardness improved between HV 300 and almost HV 500 and wear decreased with time. Under tribological stress, the FCC matrix grains refined into a nanocrystalline structure, with twinning aiding grain boundary formation [ 207 ]. This dynamic grain refinement enhances wear resistance [ 207 ]. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images show the wear tracks at different sliding durations: ( a ) 5 min, ( b ) 10 min, and ( c ) 20 min [ 188 ]

Wear in HEAs is linked to progressive subsurface oxidation, where mechanical mixing of the alloy and oxides occurs [ 159 ]. Studies reveal an oxygen-enriched layer beneath the worn surface due to re-deposited oxides [ 189 ]. Atom probe tomography shows irregularly shaped oxygen-rich regions, with high Mn and Cr content but low Fe, Co, and Ni. This suggests that reactive elements like Mn and Cr promote oxidation. Wear in Cantor alloys is primarily caused by delamination from plastic deformation. Additionally, nanocrystalline and plastically deformed layer forms, increasing hardness and enhancing wear resistance [ 189 ].

The Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi) primarily exhibits a face-centered cubic (FCC) phase, which is a common structure in HEAs [ 57 ]. Much of the research reviewed explores how to modify or add elements to shift from FCC to body-centered cubic (BCC) phases.

Based on Guo’s theory of valence electron concentration (VEC), materials with a VEC above 8 tend to form simple FCC phases [ 208 ]. In FCC crystals, atoms have more neighboring atoms, leading to an increased number of slip systems. This reduces hardness and wear resistance but enhances ductility in FCC phase-dominant HEAs [ 208 ].

The (CoCrFeMnNi)85Ti15 coating demonstrates excellent wear resistance at elevated temperatures, particularly at 400 °C. In both HECs, wear resistance increases with temperature up to 400 °C but decreases thereafter. Figure  8 (a-b) presents the friction coefficient of CoCrFeMnNi and (CoCrFeMnNi)85Ti15 coatings over a range of temperatures with respect to wear time [ 197 ]. Recent studies indicate that the tribocorrosion behavior of CoCrFeMnNi High-Entropy Alloy (Cantor Alloy) remains less explored compared with its dry sliding wear performance. Preliminary investigations suggest that compositionally modified CoCrFeNi-based High-Entropy Alloys and additively manufactured or laser-cladded coatings are promising candidates for future tribocorrosion studies due to their refined microstructures and improved passivation behavior in chloride environments [ 209 ,  210 ].

Another tribocorrosion study reported that the addition of Al and Mo significantly reduces corrosion-induced wear damage of HEAs in artificial seawater [ 211 ]. Similarly, in the case of Al0.1CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy, Al addition considerably improved wear resistance compared with CoCrFeMnNi High-Entropy Alloy under both dry and marine environments [ 212 ]. Furthermore, additively manufactured CoCrFeMnNi High-Entropy Alloy exhibited superior tribocorrosion resistance against an Al₂O₃ (Aluminum Oxide) ball due to its refined microstructure and stable passive film. These results indicate that additive manufacturing techniques significantly enhances wear resistance and tribocorrosion performance compared with conventional production methods such as Arc Melting [ 213 ].

Standardization of key parameters—including electrolyte composition (e.g., 3.5 wt% Sodium Chloride (NaCl) solution), electrochemical monitoring during sliding, applied load, and counter-body material—is essential for meaningful comparison among studies and for understanding the synergy between wear and corrosion [ 209 ,  210 ]. Such standardization would facilitate systematic comparisons among different HEA compositions and processing routes and accelerate the development of structure–property relationships governing tribocorrosion behavior in Cantor-alloy-derived systems.

A comparison of tribological properties reported for CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys processed by different techniques is summarized in Table  3 , highlighting the strong influence of microstructure and processing conditions on wear performance. From Table  3 , the wear rates of various HEAs carried out in the air at room temperature (RT) wear conditions, highlighting their resistance to wear and enabling a discussion on how microstructural evolution influences their tribological properties. Even under different wear conditions, the Cantor alloy demonstrates relatively poor wear resistance, with wear rates between 8× 10⁻⁵ and 56 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/(N•m) [ 57 ,  182 ,  188 ,  189 ]. Similarly, CoCrFeNi alloys, a key variant of the Cantor alloy, also exhibit high wear rates, ranging from 23× 10⁻⁵ to 136 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/(N•m) [ 190 ,  191 ,  214 ,  215 ].

There are different methods that are examined to increase the wear resistance of these single-phase fcc HEAs. To begin with, CoCrFeNi alloyed with Mo does not have a significant effect on the enhancement of wear resistance as the fcc phase is not altered [ 190 ]. Secondly, conversion of fcc stage to bcc brings about a great reduction in wear rates [ 57 ]. For example, the bcc-structured CoCrFeNiAl HEA exhibits a wear rate of 8 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/(N-m), which is merely one-third of that observed in CoCrFeNiAl₀.₃ HEA (24 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/(N-m)) that retains an fcc phase [ 57 ]. Thirdly, incorporation of hard intermetallic particles in the HEA matrix contributes significantly to wear resistance [ 182 ,  213 ,  216 ]. For example, adding 40 wt% Cr₂C₃ to the Cantor alloy reduces the wear rate from 56× 10⁻⁵ to 0.49 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/(N•m) [ 182 ]. Finally, it can be significantly used to reduce wear loss by forming a hardening layer or a self-lubricating microstructure which can reduce wear rates by more than an order of magnitude [ 191 ,  214 ,  217 ].

Figure  9  indicates that the wear process changes with time. First, the worn surface is subjected to plastic deformation by abrasion and adhesion producing a thin layer of deformed surface with a layer of wear debris. The oxidation of the wear material on the surface occurs due to frictional heating as the sliding continues. These oxidized particles serve as a lubricating layer and they reduce the rate of friction as well as wear with time [ 188 ]. sections.heading: The role of external factors in modifying the tribological properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs
paragraphs: The tribological properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs are strongly influenced by external factors, particularly elemental composition and proportion, which significantly affect their wear resistance and erosion performance in oil and gas components [ 218 ].

This Section discusses the influence of external factors on tribological behavior. Microstructure-mediated effects, primarily governed by processing routes, and composition-driven effects, where alloying additions (external elements additions) alter phase stability, tribological behavior, and wear mechanisms.

sections.heading: Factors influence on tribological properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs
paragraphs: Alloying and thermomechanical treatments enhance strength through precipitation hardening, grain boundary hardening, twinning, transformation hardening, and surface treatment [ 219 ,  220 – 221 ].

Grain size, carbide precipitation, and element addition have an impact on the tribology of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs [ 58 ,  222 ]. Experimental methods of tribological behavior of HEAs are the analysis of the sliding experiment and the morphology of the worn surfaces [ 58 ,  222 ] of different grain size. HfO 2  addition has the ability to enhance hardness of the HEAs [ 119 ]. Furthermore, the tribological characteristics of HEAs that contain high concentrations of solute atoms are better [ 159 ]. Laser energy density of laser cladding is also an important factor in wear and corrosion resistance; a certain energy density shows an outstanding performance [ 223 ,  224 ].

CoCrFeMnNi HEAs are attracting attention since they have superior wear and corrosion resistance properties [ 225 ]. Assessing their wear performance is crucial for evaluating their overall durability [ 58 ].

sections.heading: Impact of temperature
paragraphs: Protective oxide layers on HEA surfaces enhance wear resistance by lowering friction as temperature rises. The (CoCrFeMnNi)₈₅Ti₁₅ HEA coating demonstrated superior wear resistance at elevated temperatures [ 197 ]. while the CoCrFeMnNi alloy performed best at moderate temperatures [ 226 ] [ 226 ]. CoCrFeMnNi HEAs fabricated by Fast Hot-Pressed Sintering (FHP) at different temperatures retained a single-phase FCC structure, while grain size increased with higher sintering temperature. Above 900 °C, the alloy achieved high density and good mechanical properties, though hardness slightly decreased due to grain growth. During sliding against Al₂O₃ balls, the alloy showed good wear resistance, mainly governed by oxidative and abrasive wear mechanisms [ 227 ].

The temperature-dependent wear behavior of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs generally shows three regimes shown in Fig.  10 , temperature regimes and effect on wear mechanism, and corresponding characteristics are summarized in Table  4 . The temperature-dependent wear behavior of the Cantor alloy CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy can be divided into three regimes. At room temperature (RT), sliding wear produces severe plastic deformation and nanocrystalline grain refinement beneath the worn surface [ 159 ,  228 ].At ~ 600 °C, precipitation of the hard σ phase and refined FCC grains significantly reduce the wear rate [ 228 ]. However, at ~ 800 °C, recrystallization and grain coarsening decrease wear resistance [ 57 ]. The wear mechanism also shifts from abrasive wear at RT to oxidation wear with delamination above ~ 600 °C [ 57 ,  229 ].Overall, the alloy shows wear rates of 8 × 10⁻⁵ to 56 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/(N·m), slightly higher than those of 316 stainless steel, AISI 304 steel, and Inconel 718 under similar conditions [ 57 ,  182 ,  188 ,  189 ,  215 ].The wear map follows the principles of Oxidative Wear, where moderate oxidation forms a protective film, but excessive oxidation at higher temperatures leads to scale fracture and increased wear. The wear mechanism in High-Entropy Alloys shifts from abrasive wear at room temperature to oxidative and delamination wear at elevated temperatures, where protective oxide films reduce friction [ 230 ]. Consequently, HEAs exhibit higher wear resistance than AISI 304 Stainless Steel above 300 °C and Inconel 718 above 800 °C due to the formation of protective oxide layers [ 57 ].

sections.heading: Surface modification
paragraphs: Surface treatments can further improve alloy properties for CoCrFeMnNiHEAs [ 231 ]. Wear resistance is improved by induced oxidation and subsurface grain refinement [ 188 ]. In CoCrFeMnNi HEAs with varying morphology densities, scratch deformation primarily occurs through slip facilitated by Shockley partial dislocations [ 232 ].

Surface modification significantly improves the tribological properties of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Composite coatings show enhanced performance at 800–1000 °C [ 39 ]. A surface design strategy, combining coating technologies and surface modification, helps reduce HEA cost while improving surface properties [ 233 ,  234 ,  235 – 236 ]. Techniques such as plasma nitriding increase surface hardness and wear resistance, though corrosion behavior depends on treatment temperature [ 236 ]. Additionally, ultrasonic shot peening (USP) enhances tribological performance from room temperature to 600 °C [ 36 ], while WC particle-reinforced HEA coatings significantly improve wear resistance [ 237 ].

sections.heading: Lubrication effects
paragraphs: The HEA presents better tribological properties due to the formation of more lubricating oxides induced by the tribo-pair [ 55 ]. A composite exhibited excellent tribological properties attributed to the synergistic lubricating effect of graphite and MoS [ 191 ]. The lubrication effect of Al x CoCrFeMnNi cladding layer with MoS 2 has a synergistic effect [ 238 ].

Lubrication effects significantly enhance the tribological performance of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Boriding combined with glycerol lubrication can achieve superlubricity, producing a near-zero friction coefficient (~ 0.003) and ultra-low wear rate (~ 10⁻⁷ mm³/N·m) due to the formation of a boron-ester tribofilm during tribochemical reactions [ 239 ]. Additionally, surface texturing improves the wear resistance of CoCrNi and CoCrFeMnNi alloys [ 240 ], while CoCrFeMnNi–SiC nanocomposites reduce wear and oxidation through a self-lubricating effect during sliding [ 43 ].

sections.heading: Influence of aluminium (Al)
paragraphs: Aluminum significantly increases the yield strength and hardness of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs by promoting the formation of a FCC phase, which balances strength and ductility [ 243 ,  252 ].

Increasing Al content led to a structural shift from FCC to BCC, significantly improving hardness and compressive yield strength from 1.59 GPa to 3.73 GPa, while fracture strain declined from 20.91% (no fracture) to 13.78%. The presence of nanotwins and BCC phase contributed to strengthening in CoCrFeMnNiAl x  HEAFs. The film exhibited better hardness and strength than the bulk counterparts because the grain size was smaller and there was a presence of nanotwin [ 243 ]. An increase in the concentration of Al enhanced the Primitive Cubic (PC) phase fraction, which further enhanced mechanical properties. The CoCrFeNiMn 5 Al 15  alloy recorded the highest value of hardness of 6684 HV, compressive yield strength of 2135 Mpa, and ultimate compressive strength of 2496 Mpa [ 244 ]. Individual yield strengths may be of a remarkable high level, where CoCrFeMnNiAl 0.75  may have a maximum yield strength of 1.194 GPa and 1.2 GPa may be achieved in higher levels of aluminum additives [ 243 ,  244 ].
Addiding more Al content increased the hardness from 493 ± 3 HV1 (Mn 15 Al 5 ) to 668 ± 4 HV1 (Mn 5 Al 15 ), surpassing the quinary equiatomic CoCrFeNiAl alloy, which reached only 646 HV [ 244 ].

sections.heading: Role of Chromium (Cr)
paragraphs: Chromium plays an important role in improving the microhardness and tensile strength of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. Cr alloys containing 1.3 at% Cr contain a microhardness of 217.8 HV0.5 and tensile strength of 691 MPa. The hardening effect of Cr of solid solution enhances the plasticity and the overall mechanical performance of the solid solution and elevates the structural stability at stress [ 103 ].
Electrochemical corrosion experiments indicate that Cr content is able to greatly increase the corrosion resistance of the alloy in question [ 103 ] with a rise in Cr content.

sections.heading: Influence of Nickel (Ni)
paragraphs: Nickel also increases the hardness and strength of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs, which results in high ductility at low temperatures. It helps develop a strong microstructure which is resistant to degradation, albeit increasing the Ni content will complicate the performance [ 253 ].

The addition of Ni leads to serious lattice distortion which increases solid solution hardening and influences alloy responses. By choosing and optimizing external factors in CoCrFeMnNi HEAs, one can make a significant improvement in the mechanical properties, and trade-offs between ductility and brittle behavior may be resolved [ 253 ]. Ni in HEAs segregates to the surface during friction, forming a Ni-rich oxidized layer. This creates a nanocomposite oxide layer that improves plastic flow and wear resistance [ 254 ].

sections.heading: Influence of Carbon (C)
paragraphs: The C-HEA-V200 had yield and tensile strength of about 829 Mpa and 989Mpa respectively and total elongation of roughly 24.3%. C-HEA-V600 also demonstrated a yield strength of approximately 741 MPa and tensile strength of 874 Mpa though overall elongation became slightly lower 39.7% as compared to 45.7% in as-cast samples. It is worth noting that C-HEA-V200 was stronger than C-HEA-V600 though it had a large grain size. The addition of a low concentration of carbon was found to be able to improve the mechanical properties of the HEAs processed by SLM, and the as-built HEAs of 1% C-CoCrFeMnNi were found to be much stronger than CoCrFeMnNi HEAs. The small manufacturing method has allowed the high-tensile strength of as-built C-HEA, which has been attained using several mechanisms of strengthening (solid solution, grain refinement, dislocation density, and nano-precipitation). The SLM process was able to reinforce maximally the addition of carbon, through the finely dispersed nano-carbides at the edges of the solidification cellular structure [ 102 ].

The CrFeCoNiMnCx (x = 0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2) with a carbon-free structure has a significantly rough surface caused by the existence of a soft and brittle FCC structure. Pitting occurs in locations where the debris has broken loose, which means that delamination wear is the prevailing mechanism [ 193 ]. However, with the addition of 0.6 moles of carbon, delamination wear is no longer observed. This improvement in surface durability is attributed to the precipitation of M₇C₃ carbides, which enhance wear resistance in CrFeCoNiMnC₀.₆. As the carbon content increases to 1.2, the wear mechanism shifts to abrasive wear, characterized by deep grooves and micro-cracks on the surface [ 193 ].

sections.heading: Influence of Niobium (Nb)
paragraphs: An increment in the oxidation temperature improves segregation of Nb and Laves phase. Precipitation of Laves phase at the scale/alloy interface of Nb0.25 alloy enhances the oxidation resistance by inhibiting the active diffusion of cation metals whereas internal Laves phase permits the internal diffusion of oxygen ion, resulting in internal oxidation. Consequently, the Nb0.25 alloy has a better oxidation resistance than the Nb0 alloy at 700 and 800 °C, but the opposite at 900 C. Therefore, Nb has a dual role in the oxidation process [ 130 ].

sections.heading: Influence of Silicon (Si)
paragraphs: Silicon (Si) substitution in CoCrFeMnNi HEA (e.g., Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Mn10Si10) enhances yield strength and ultimate tensile strength compared with the Cantor alloy, though the initial elongation slightly decreases. After solution treatment, both strength and ductility significantly improve due to mechanisms such as TWIP effect, Peierls–Nabarro stress, and grain-boundary strengthening. Si addition also increases electrical resistivity and lowers TCR, attributed to lattice distortion and structural fluctuations, making Si-alloyed HEAs promising for structural–functional and electrothermal applications [ 246 ]. Si additions significantly influence phase stability and wear resistance in cantor alloy and HEA coatings [ 255 ,  256 ].

sections.heading: Influence of Titanium (Ti)
paragraphs: Titanium (Ti) addition in CoCrFeMnNi HEAs promotes the formation of hard secondary phases and increases lattice distortion, leading to improved strength, hardness, and wear resistance [ 257 ,  258 ]. Ti-containing alloys often form intermetallic phases (e.g., Laves phases) and refined microstructures, which enhance microhardness and reduce wear rate and friction coefficient [ 241 ]. However, increasing Ti content may also increase porosity, reduce oxidation and corrosion resistance, indicating a trade-off between improved mechanical/tribological properties and electrochemical stability [ 242 ].

sections.heading: Influence of Molybdenum (Mo)
paragraphs: Microstructure formation in CoFeNiMnMox alloys is governed by atomic size difference (δ) and ΔχA, with criteria δ ≥ 3.87% and ΔχA ≥ 5.24 effectively predicting the coexistence of the (FCC + Laves) phase. Increasing Mo content raises δ and decreases valence electron concentration (VEC), indicating significant lattice distortion and structural instability. XRD and SEM analyses show that the microstructures consist of FCC and Laves phases. Compressive strengths for the alloys are: Mo0.25 (187 MPa), Mo0.50 (261 MPa), Mo0.75 (394 MPa), and Mo1.00 (531MPa) [ 245 ] in Table  5 . Mo in HEAs promotes defect accumulation and rapid friction-induced amorphization, especially at low temperatures. The formed hard amorphous layer reduces strain and cracking, improving wear resistance [ 259 ].

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: In this review different fabrication methods and their impact of processing techniques on phase formation, microstructure and tribological properties are discussed. Based on this high entropy alloys (HEAs) can be shaped to meet diverse application need across industry and material engineering. This review consolidates the causal chain from fabrication route to phase constitution and wear response in CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs and their coatings. The harmonized evidence base demonstrates that purposeful phase control—especially FCC→BCC transitions and intermetallic or carbide reinforcement—delivers predictable reductions in wear across comparable contact conditions. Processing route dictates phase selection (FCC→BCC/σ/Laves) and defect structures; these, in turn, govern hardness, friction and wear (at room and elevated temperatures). Normalized data exhibit multi-fold reductions in wear due to either conversion of FCC to BCC or the addition of hard intermetallics/carbides, the addition of solid lubricants also enhances friction stability especially in high temperatures conditions. A wide range of coating reduces the material wear in the range of about 400 °C, at which point the harder tribo-oxide coating has been developed. Above 400 °C, the coarser tribo-oxide coating can eliminate the benefits. Designs that take advantage of lubricious oxide films can achieve low friction around ~ 400 °C, but higher temperature exposure requires mitigation of scale breakdown through composition, architecture (e.g., multilayers or graded coatings), and controlled oxygen activity. This is a practical implication of route selection guided by service temperature. The present study also includes the detailed analysis of tribology of single- and multi-phase high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and their composites at the room temperature (RT) and high temperatures (ET), which resulted in the following major findings:

The processing routes have a significant influence on the microstructure, properties and performance of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloys (HEAs). Such methods as conventional casting, melt-spinning, mechanical alloying, selective laser melting and laser powder bed fusion give a variety of grain structures, strength and durability. Such effects are important to understand in order to optimize the HEA properties to be used in certain applications. Microstructure, mechanical and tribological characteristics of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloys (HEAs) are greatly affected by external factors and elements. Strength and ductility can be improved by addition of such elements as aluminum (Al), copper (Cu), chromium (Cr), and manganese (Mn), whereas others are likely to cause brittle properties or low ductility, which must be carefully considered in the design of alloys. Face centred cubic single-phase HEA would normally possess low hardness and low wear resistance, however the addition of hard particles in the material would substantially improve their wear characteristics. The high temperature tribological characteristics of HEAs are remarkable and are largely attributed to the evolution of the microstructure on the subsurface, the formation of oxide layers, and the high resistance to softening. Heat treatment and Surface hardening treatments have been shown to provide primary hardness and wear resistance in HEAs whereas remelting, cold rolling and annealing processes are much more effective in increasing wear resistance. Self-lubricating HEAs have the potential of being used in tribology because they are capable of obtaining low friction coefficients, and lower wear rates. Friction and wear resistance are tribological properties that are influenced by temperature. Higher impact angles generally reduce erosion, and wear properties are highly environment dependent. The effect of alloying elements (Al, Ti, Mo, Nb) on corrosion resistance varies based on composition, concentration, and environmental conditions, with no universal rule. HEAs can replace conventional alloys in high-wear and corrosion-prone applications, such as aerospace moving components, dies, molds, cutting tools, engines, structural components, pipelines, and acid pumps, potentially extending component lifespan. Since AM alloys’ homogeneous chemistry and reduced porosity already correlate with better corrosion resistance, further research should compare coupled tribocorrosion metrics (such as in-situ current density under sliding) for AM vs. cast CoCrFeMnNi.

Overall, CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs demonstrate significant potential as wear-resistant materials for demanding engineering environments. Continued research focusing on microstructure optimization, advanced manufacturing methods, and standardized tribological testing will further advance the development of these alloys for practical applications in aerospace, energy, and manufacturing industries.

HEAs have a lot of potential as next-generation wear-resistant materials because of their exceptional qualities, which include high hardness, wear resistance, corrosion resistance, temperature stability, oxidation resistance, and softening resistance. Numerous potentials use in tribology are suggested by the fact that some HEAs already perform better tribologically than traditional alloys. In the future, researchers can intentionally create HEAs suited for wear-resistant applications because of the wide variety of potential alloy compositions.

sections.heading: Recommendations for processing routes
paragraphs: Controlling the processing path is essential to preserving the mechanical properties of HEAs by reducing the production of brittle precipitates, especially the σ-phase. A better processing method is Selective Laser Melting (SLM), which is aimed at the quality of surfaces and dimensionality, and the generation of minimal amounts of brittle precipitates in high-entropy alloys. It is also effective to enhance tensile strength, thermal stability, corrosion resistance, yield strength and microstructural control.

sections.heading: Recommendations for improving tribological properties
paragraphs: The analysis of element ratio in tribological characteristics of multi-component alloys may contribute to the creation of new HEAs/MEAs possessing optimal tribological characteristics. By adding carbide by flake powder metallurgy, tribological characteristics of HEAs can be improved. The issues of improving the wear resistance of HEAs require future research. The tribological study of varying grain sizes of CoCrFeMnNi HEAs can be used to gain systematic knowledge according to the sliding experiments and the morphology of the worn surface.
Although these developments have been made, there are still a few challenges in this field:

It is yet to be investigated into the atomic-scale mechanisms that control wear resistance in HEAs, and the role that precipitates play in determining the softening resistance of alloys at high temperatures. Although the wear mechanisms of Cantor alloy-based HEAs are not still researched, the investigation of the basic tribological principles of body-centered cubic (bcc) refractory HEAs still requires some research.
